summary: This document specifies a DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 option carrying the civic location of the client or the DHCP server, such as country, state or province, city, street address and building details. It allows several renditions of one address in different scripts and languages. It was replaced by RFC 4776.

plainLanguage.summary: When your computer joins a network, it can be told the street address of where it is. This option carries that address, even in several languages. It was later replaced by RFC 4776.

subtitle: Telling devices where they are using DHCP configuration

tldr.problem: IP phones and other networked devices need to know their physical address to contact emergency services and be located by responders, but there was no standard way to convey this information.
tldr.mechanism: A new DHCP option (code 99 for DHCPv4, code 37 for DHCPv6) carries civic address information including country, state, city, and street details, supporting multiple languages and scripts.
tldr.outcome: Devices can now reliably discover their street addresses via DHCP, though the specification was replaced by RFC 4776 for technical improvements.

today: RFC 4676 is a Proposed Standard that was superseded by RFC 4776, which refined the specification based on implementation experience.

sections.title: Location for Emergency Response
sections.content:
IP telephony devices (like Voice over IP phones) need to know their physical location to contact the correct emergency response agency when someone calls 911 or the local equivalent. A device in Chicago needs to reach Chicago's emergency dispatcher, not one in New York.

There are two common ways to express location: geospatial coordinates (longitude, latitude, altitude) and civic addresses (street addresses). This RFC defines how to deliver civic addresses via DHCP. The approach treats DHCP as a sighting function similar to a GPS receiver wired to a network node, delivering location information from a trusted server to clients in controlled environments.

The same address information is often represented in multiple languages and scripts. For example, Munich is called Muenchen in German and Monaco in Italian. This option supports all these renditions so that emergency responders or presence systems can use the appropriate language for their context.
sections.plainLanguage: When your phone connects to a network, the network tells it the address of where it is. This helps emergency services find you and helps your presence information show the right language.

sections.title: How the Option Works
sections.content:
For DHCPv4, the option is code 99 (GEOCONF_CIVIC). For DHCPv6, it is code 37 (OPTION_GEOCONF_CIVIC). Both versions contain three parts: a what field (indicating whether the information describes the server, the nearest network element, or the client), a country code (a two-letter ISO 3166 country code like US or DE), and a series of civic address elements.

Each address element is a type-length-value structure with a CAtype (Civic Address type) number, a length, and a value. The types include standard elements like country (CAtype 1 for states or provinces), city (CAtype 3), street address (CAtype 34), postal code (CAtype 24), building (CAtype 25), and more specialized elements like room number (CAtype 28) or seat (CAtype 33).

Language and script information can be specified to mark different renditions of the same address. When a language tag (CAtype 0) or script tag (CAtype 128) appears, it applies to subsequent elements until overridden by another tag. This allows the DHCP server to provide the same address in German, English, and Italian, for example.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is a list of address pieces. Each piece has a type number (like 3 for city), the text, and optional language tags to say what language it is.

sections.title: Address Elements and Structure
sections.content:
The RFC defines a hierarchical approach to address components, recognizing that civic hierarchies differ from country to country. The specification includes five levels of administrative subdivisions (A1 through A5, such as state, county, city, city district, neighborhood) plus detailed mappings for major countries. For the United States, A1 is the state, A2 is the county, and A3 is the civic community name. For Germany, A1 is the state (Bundesstaat), A2 is the administrative region, A3 is the city, and A4 is the district.

Beyond the administrative hierarchy, the option includes street-level details: primary road name (CAtype 34), house number (CAtype 19), house number suffix (CAtype 20), building name (CAtype 25), unit or apartment (CAtype 26), floor (CAtype 27), room (CAtype 28), and various street modifiers. A landmark or vanity address (CAtype 21) like a university name can also be specified.

For postal addresses, the option supports postal code (CAtype 24), postal community name (CAtype 30, for cases where the postal delivery name differs from the civic name), and post office box (CAtype 31). Additional country-specific codes (CAtype 32) like Japan's JIS address code allow finer granularity within a country.
sections.plainLanguage: The address is broken into pieces: country, state, city, street, house number, building, unit, room. Each country organizes these differently, so the option handles variations.

sections.title: Privacy and Authentication
sections.content:
Location information is sensitive. The RFC specifies that DHCP servers SHOULD only return the civic address option if the client explicitly requested it (by including the option code in its parameter request list). This prevents servers from leaking location data to clients that do not expect it.

DHCP traffic is not encrypted, so anyone monitoring the link between the DHCP server and client can see the location information. Therefore, this option should only be used on networks with access restrictions or network-layer privacy mechanisms. For critical decisions based on location, DHCPv4 authentication (RFC 3118) SHOULD be used to protect the integrity of the DHCP option.

Once a client obtains location information via DHCP, it must afford the information the protections defined in RFC 3694. Location information SHOULD NOT be sent from client to server, because that would grant the server unlimited retention and distribution permissions.
sections.plainLanguage: Location is sensitive, so servers should only send it if asked. Networks should be secure so no one eavesdrops. Use DHCP authentication for critical uses.

sections.title: Example: A Munich Address
sections.content:
The RFC includes an example of Munich city hall in Bavaria, Germany, expressed in German, English, and Italian. In German (language tag de, script tag Latn for Latin), it specifies Bayern (Bavaria) as A1, Oberbayern as A2, München as A3, Marienplatz as the street (CAtype 6), house number 8, the landmark Rathaus (town hall), postal code 80331, and the type of place as government-building. The same location is then restated with the English names (Bavaria, Munich) and Italian names (Baviera, Monaco), with the understanding that non-language-specific elements like the house number and postal code apply across all language variants.

This illustrates how the option handles multilingual addresses efficiently: common elements appear once, while language-specific variants are added when they differ. The structure allows emergency services to select the language and level of detail appropriate for their context.
sections.plainLanguage: One address can be listed multiple times in different languages. Common details like the house number are shared; only the language-specific parts (city names, state names) are repeated.

fields.name: What
fields.desc: Indicates server (0), network element (1), or client (2) location

fields.name: Country Code
fields.desc: Two-letter ISO 3166 country code (e.g., US, DE)
